beats.title: Purgatorius, Early Primate Kin
beats.description: A tiny, shrew-sized tree-climber appeared just after the asteroid, a close kin of every later monkey and ape.
beats.note: Oldest remains about 65.9 Ma; rounded to 66 Ma.

beats.title: Plesiadapis, Squirrel-Like Primate
beats.description: A squirrel-sized, long-clawed climber lived in forests of two continents and is among the first primate-like mammals.
beats.note: Genus range 58-55 Ma.

beats.title: Coryphodon, the Swamp Giant
beats.description: A hippo-sized, tusked swamp browser with a tiny brain was one of the largest mammals of its warm, wet world.
beats.note: Recalled from reference range (about 56 Ma); not separately searched.

beats.title: Eohippus, the Dawn Horse
beats.description: A fox-sized, four-toed forest browser stands at the base of the horse family tree.
beats.note: Year per theme example; sources vary 56-55 Ma.

beats.title: Icaronycteris, an Early Bat
beats.description: A fully winged, insect-hunting bat left skeletons in a Wyoming lake bed, already able to fly and echolocate.
beats.note: Oldest bat skeletons, about 52 Ma.

beats.title: Uintatherium, the Horned Giant
beats.description: A rhino-sized plant eater carried three pairs of bony knobs and long, downward-pointing canine tusks.
beats.note: Wikipedia range 50.5-37 Ma; sources vary.

beats.title: Pakicetus, Walking Whale Ancestor
beats.description: A wolf-sized, hoofed hunter living beside rivers has ear bones that mark it as an early relative of whales.
beats.note: Sources 48-52 Ma; about 50 used.

beats.title: Ambulocetus, the Walking Whale
beats.description: A crocodile-like, short-legged ambusher could both paddle and walk, caught midway between land and sea.
beats.note: Year per theme example; not separately searched.

beats.title: Andrewsarchus, Giant Hoofed Hunter
beats.description: A massive skull from the Mongolian desert shows a wolf-like, hoofed meat eater bigger than any bear.
beats.note: Range 47.8-42.7 Ma; about 45 Ma (AMNH figure).

beats.title: Basilosaurus, the Serpent Whale
beats.description: A fully ocean-going, snake-bodied whale grew to about 18 metres and still carried tiny hind legs.
beats.note: Year per theme example; not separately searched.

beats.title: Hyaenodon, Early Meat-Eater
beats.description: A long-snouted, hyena-toothed hunter ranged across two continents for a very long stretch, preying on early grazers.
beats.note: Wikipedia genus range 38-11.4 Ma.

beats.title: Moeritherium, Early Elephant Kin
beats.description: A swamp-dwelling, tapir-like animal with short tusks sits at the base of the elephant family.
beats.note: Most sources 37-35 Ma.

beats.title: Arsinoitherium, Two-Horned Giant
beats.description: A rhino-like African giant carried two enormous, cone-shaped horns side by side on its snout.
beats.note: Range 36-30 Ma.

beats.title: Dinictis, the False Sabre-Tooth
beats.description: A lithe, cat-sized stalker with long upper canines hunted in North American woods, though it was not a true cat.
beats.note: Current Wikipedia range 35.7-29.5 Ma; older mirrors differ.

beats.title: Paraceratherium, Land Giant
beats.description: A hornless, long-necked rhino relative stood taller than a giraffe and weighed as much as several elephants.
beats.note: Year per theme example.

beats.title: Aegyptopithecus, Dawn Monkey
beats.description: A cat-sized, tree-living early ape relative left a skull in the Egyptian desert, near the root of apes and monkeys.
beats.why_in: early anthropoid primate, not a human species
beats.note: Range 38-29.5 Ma; revised dating 30.2-29.5 Ma; about 30 used.

beats.title: Desmostylus, the Odd Sea Grazer
beats.description: A hippo-like coastal mammal with bundled, column-shaped teeth grazed seaweed along North Pacific shores.
beats.note: Wikipedia genus range 28.4-7.25 Ma.

beats.title: Proconsul, Early Ape of Africa
beats.description: A tailless, monkey-sized tree-dweller in East African forests is among the earliest known apes.
beats.why_in: early ape, not a human species
beats.note: Oldest record about 23.5 Ma (Meswa Bridge); genus range often given 21-17 Ma.

beats.title: Daeodon, the Hell Pig
beats.description: A bear-sized, pig-like omnivore with a huge head and bone-crushing teeth stalked the open North American plains.
beats.note: Sources 23-18 Ma; start used.

beats.title: Amphicyon, the Bear Dog
beats.description: A heavy, bear-sized hunter with a dog-like head was among the top predators of its continents.
beats.note: Genus range about 20.6-9 Ma; low-authority source.

beats.title: Gomphotherium, Four-Tusked Giant
beats.description: A four-tusked, elephant-like browser left Africa and spread across the northern continents.
beats.note: Oldest remains about 19.5 Ma in Africa.

beats.title: Merychippus, the Grazing Horse
beats.description: A pony-sized horse with tall, hard-wearing teeth began feeding on the grasses of spreading prairies.
beats.note: Recalled from reference range (about 17 Ma); not separately searched.

beats.title: Chalicotherium, the Clawed Browser
beats.description: A horse-like head sat on a gorilla-like body, with huge claws instead of hooves for pulling down branches.
beats.note: Genus given as Middle to Late Miocene; sources disagree widely, about 16 Ma used as approximate start.

beats.title: Platybelodon, the Shovel-Tusker
beats.description: An elephant relative with flattened lower tusks scooped up and stripped plants like a living shovel.
beats.note: Recalled from reference range (about 15 Ma); not separately searched.

beats.title: Deinotherium, Downturned Tusks
beats.description: A giant elephant relative had tusks curving downward from its lower jaw and stood about four metres tall.
beats.note: Year per theme example; genus fossils reach older in some sources.

beats.title: Livyatan, the Giant Sperm Whale
beats.description: A huge-toothed whale hunted other whales off the coast of what is now Peru.
beats.note: Revised dating 9.9-8.9 Ma; older sources say 12-13 Ma.

beats.title: Thylacosmilus, Pouched Sabre-Tooth
beats.description: A South American pouched predator grew sabre-like canines like a cat's, though it was no cat.
beats.note: Sources say roughly 10-3 Ma; 9 used as approximate start of T. atrox.

beats.title: Sivatherium, the Giant Giraffe
beats.description: A heavy, moose-like relative of giraffes carried two pairs of horns, one pair broad and branching.
beats.note: Originated about 7 Ma.

beats.title: Megatherium, the Giant Ground Sloth
beats.description: An elephant-sized, clawed leaf eater of South America reared up on its hind legs to reach branches.
beats.note: Year per theme example.

beats.title: Josephoartigasia, the Giant Rodent
beats.description: A South American relative of the guinea pig grew to the size of a bull, the biggest rodent on record.
beats.note: Recalled from reference range (about 4-2 Ma); not separately searched.

beats.title: Smilodon, the Sabre-Tooth
beats.description: A stocky, powerful big cat with knife-like upper canines ambushed large prey across the Americas.
beats.note: Year per theme example.

beats.title: Glyptodon, the Armoured Giant
beats.description: A car-sized relative of armadillos wore a solid domed shell of fused bony plates.
beats.note: Sources give about 2-2.5 Ma start; 2 used to avoid clashing with Smilodon.

beats.title: Arctodus, Giant Short-Faced Bear
beats.description: A long-legged North American bear stood taller than a grizzly and may have been the largest meat-eating bear.
beats.note: Recalled from reference range (about 1.8 Ma); not separately searched.

beats.title: Diprotodon, the Giant Wombat
beats.description: A rhino-sized pouched grazer, the largest marsupial ever, wandered Australia in herds.
beats.note: Recalled from reference range (about 1.6 Ma); not separately searched.

beats.title: Cave Lion, the Ice Age Big Cat
beats.description: A huge, pale cat larger than any living lion hunted across the cold steppes, and was painted by early artists.
beats.note: Recalled from reference range (roughly 600-700 ka); not separately searched.

beats.title: Woolly Mammoth
beats.description: A shaggy, long-tusked elephant, adapted to freezing grassland, became the best-known beast of the cold steppe.
beats.note: Sources range 400,000-750,000 years; theme example 400,000 used.

beats.title: Cave Bear, the Cavern Dweller
beats.description: A huge, plant-eating bear spent winters hibernating in caves across Europe, leaving bones in vast numbers.
beats.note: Recalled from reference range (about 300 ka); not separately searched.

beats.title: Dire Wolf
beats.description: A heavy, big-headed wolf hunted horses and bison in the Americas alongside the sabre-tooth.
beats.note: NPS gives oldest record about 250,000 years; Wikipedia range starts 125,000.
